Griffiths

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a drawing, not a game: as a dot slides along a straight line, the circle drawn from where it meets the sides keeps passing through the same spot.
How to play: Drag A₁, A₂, A₃, P or Q, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick Perpendiculars or Circles to show the guide lines, the circles and their meeting spot.
Look for the math

Here is a theorem published by Griffiths in 1857. Put a triangle in a circle, choose a straight line through the circle's centre, and slide a point along that line. The circle you get from that point keeps going through one fixed place. That place is called the Griffiths point.

Three circles, one shared dot

Drop a perpendicular from a point to each side of the triangle. The three landing spots sit on a circle, called the pedal circle of that point. The triangle's side midpoints and other notable spots sit on the nine-point circle. Griffiths' claim, as the page puts it, is: if a point moves on a fixed line through the circumcenter, its pedal circle passes through a fixed point on the nine point circle. The applet shows two points, P and Q, on the same line through O; tick Circles to see the two pedal circles meet the nine-point circle at one dot.

Why the dot cannot move

Put the circumcenter at the origin of the complex plane, make the circle have radius 1, and turn the picture so the chosen line is the real axis. If the triangle's vertices are a₁, a₂, a₃, the shared dot is

w = (a₁ + a₂ + a₃ − a₁a₂a₃) / 2

There is no p in that formula: wherever the sliding point is on the line, w is the same. The proof shows that w lies on the pedal circle of any point of the line, and when the point is at O the pedal circle is exactly the nine-point circle. The logic test checks this formula, the fixed dot and the three-circle meeting on 179 configurations; all hold. When the sliding point is on the circumcircle itself, the three feet become a straight Simson line and there is no pedal circle to draw.

Not the other Griffiths pictures

This is one triangle and two points on a line. Four Griffiths takes four points on one circle; for each of the four triangles it marks a Griffiths point, and those four points lie on a line while the four pedal circles share a dot. Griffiths Collinearity, due to Hubert Shutrick, takes the three places where a line cuts the sides of a triangle: those three pedal circles are coaxal and their centres are collinear. These are different statements about the same construction, not the one made here.

What the port changes

The live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra figure; a 2006 Wayback capture shows the original Java applet, with width 500 and height 300 and the same claim. This port keeps its two checkboxes (both off at first) and its rules for dragging: P moves Q with the same line setting, dragging Q slides it along the line, and moving a triangle corner re-centres O and carries Q. The old code always drew the names even though the page set ShowNames=0, so names are always shown here too. Its pixel test keeps the first pair of circle meetings within √2 pixels; when P and Q are very close that can pick a near miss, and this port keeps that quirk. There is no win or loss: moving something finishes the exploration.

Try ticking Perpendiculars first, then Circles, and slide Q: watch the green dot stay fixed while the two pedal circles change shape.
